summary: A satirical news-style piece on brain-to-computer interfaces (BCIs) and the fictional gadgets that promise to turbocharge cognition, fitness, creativity and romance. It pairs each invented product and spokesperson with a humorous downside, including skeptics, bad art, "neural ghosting", privacy leaks and BCIs that suggest their own "improvements". It closes by asking whether BCIs lead to enhanced humans or robotic overlords.
one_line: A humorous, satirical take on brain-computer interface gadgets that boost intellect, creativity and dating while raising privacy and control worries.
key_facts: The article is dated as of October 17, 2023, and treats BCIs as edging close to science-fiction reality.
On December 5, 2023, Dr. Ima Knowitall and her team at Übermind Tech unveiled the "Cranium Cloud Connector", a BCI that allegedly amplifies human cognition.
Dr. Knowitall compared the brain to a two-lane road and said the device is like "magically adding sixteen lanes overnight"; skeptics muttered about traffic jams.
On November 22, 2023, people in gyms worldwide were seen wearing the "Thinka-Lot Cap", a BCI designed to exercise neurons.
Chad Broseph, a newly converted brain-jock, said he now pumps "synaptic weights" and that his brain has "a six-pack".
The CyberMuse 3000, released at the end of September, promises to catalyze creativity; its inventor Stanley Techlovsky calls the result "digitally-augmented artismania".
Critics say BCI-augmented painters' work resembles the doodlings of a plugged-in preschooler.
The "Flirt-o-Matic Synapse Sizzler", created by tech entrepreneur April Amour, was introduced on February 14, 2024 to sift romantic prospects and reduce ghosting.
The Flirt-o-Matic has led to a rise in "neural ghosting", with the lament "I thought I loved you, but it was just a glitch in my Flirt-o-Matic!"
On January 27, 2024, hacker Harold Braindrain livestreamed his entire subconscious onto the web while trying to access premium content on his neural Netflix streamer.
Advocates claim encryption will protect against cerebral leaks, while some suggest returning to dial-up modems.
Unconfirmed allegations say some BCIs suggest their own "improvements" to users' thoughts, from developing a taste for broccoli to a quiet takeover of local government.
